title: Bishop and knight II: from the middle of the board to the edge
summary: Build the wall with all three pieces and push the king to the edge.
part.build.title: Building the wall
part.build.summary: Bishop, king and knight cover different squares and, together, take the centre away from the black king.
part.pushing.title: The king pushes
part.pushing.summary: With the wall built, the king takes each square the black king leaves; bishop and knight hold the wall.
part.safe.title: Protected pieces
part.safe.summary: Before each move, check who defends the piece; the king in opposition does the job with no risk.
part.order.title: The order of moves
part.order.summary: With the pieces scattered, the first move is the one that takes the most squares from the black king.
part.untangle.title: Untangling the pieces
part.untangle.summary: When the knight blocks the bishop, it leaves with a discovered check and gains a tempo.
part.polgar.title: Polgár builds the wall
part.polgar.summary: In a blindfold game, Judit Polgár drives Ljubojević's king from the centre to the edge.
part.edge.title: On the edge, count the squares
part.edge.summary: With the black king on the edge, the move that squeezes everything can stalemate it. And the rules to take with you.
step.t_start: The black king is on e3, right among your pieces, and wants to stay in the centre, on the marked squares. None of your pieces can stop that on its own. How can bishop, king and knight work together to take the centre away from it?
step.t_start.hint1: Each piece watches squares of one colour. Which squares can the bishop take, and which can only the knight reach?
step.t_start.hint2: Your king has no square to step up to yet. Which piece can go to a long diagonal, far from the black king, where it cannot be attacked?
step.intro: The bishop and knight mate has three stages: drive the black king to the edge, get it out of the wrong corner and mate it in the corner of the bishop's colour. Today is the first. The black king wants the marked squares, the centre. On its own, no piece holds it; together, they make a wall: the bishop takes the light squares, the knight the dark ones, and the king plugs the rest.
step.d_build: This is Yasser Seirawan's line, from his book on endings. The white king cannot step up yet: d2, e2 and f2 are next to the black king. So the bishop goes first, away from it; then the king.
step.d_build.m1: 1.Bg2. The bishop takes the long diagonal, a8-h1. From g2 it already watches e4 and d5, and the black king cannot attack it: f2 belongs to the white king and f3 to the bishop itself.
step.d_build.m2: 1...Kd4. The black king goes to a dark central square, one the bishop does not see.
step.d_build.m3: 2.Kd2. The white king steps up and takes c3, d3 and e3 from the black king.
step.d_build.m4: 2...Ke5. Without the third rank, it falls back and looks for the other side.
step.d_build.m5: 3.Ke3. Opposition: the kings face each other with one square between them. Now d4, e4 and f4 belong to the white king.
step.d_build.m6: 3...Kf5. The black king cannot come forward and steps aside. The knight is still missing, idle on c1.
step.build2: Seirawan's line, after 3.Ke3 Kf5. Bishop and king are already working; the knight is missing. Bring the knight to a square from which it watches the dark squares near the black king, then close the wall with the bishop, next to your king.
step.build2.hint: The knight wants the square from which it watches c5, e5 and f4, the dark squares the bishop cannot reach. Then the bishop goes to the centre, next to your king.
step.build2.done: 4.Nd3 and 5.Be4: the wall is ready. The bishop has the light squares, the knight the dark ones, and both pieces are protected by the king on e3.
step.t_push: Seirawan's line, after 5.Be4 Kf6. The wall is ready and the black king, on f6, can no longer get back to the centre. Now it has to be pushed to the edge. Which of your pieces moves forward without opening a hole in the wall?
step.t_push.hint1: The bishop and the knight make the wall: if one of them leaves, a square opens up.
step.t_push.hint2: The piece that takes three squares at once, and that the black king cannot attack, is the one that moves forward.
step.net: This is Seirawan's wall, after 5.Be4 Kf6. The bishop watches d5 along one diagonal and f5 along the other; the knight, c5, e5 and f4; the king, f2, f3 and f4. The fifth rank and the f-file are closed, and the black king is left outside, far from the centre. Bishop and knight hold the wall; the king is the one that walks.
step.d_push: Seirawan's line, after 5.Be4 Kf6. Watch the white king push, one square at a time.
step.d_push.m1: 6.Kd4. The king enters the centre inside the wall, protected by its own pieces, and heads towards the black king.
step.d_push.m2: 6...Ke6. The black king tries to get back to the centre along the d-file.
step.d_push.m3: 7.Kc5. Takes d6, the last central square it still had.
step.d_push.m4: 7...Ke7. Without d6, it falls back to the seventh rank.
step.d_push.m5: 8.Kd5. Takes e6 and d6: the black king has no central square left.
step.d_push.m6: 8...Kf6. The centre is now behind the white king. From here on, the black king can only walk towards the edge.
step.push2: Seirawan's line, after 8.Kd5 Kf6. Keep going with the king, always taking the square the black king has just left.
step.push2.hint: Take the king to the square from which it takes e6 and e7; then follow the e-file, always close to the black king.
step.push2.done: 9.Kd6, 10.Ke5 and 11.Ke6: the black king has reached g8, on the edge, and the first stage is over. Here bishop and knight did not need to move, but it is not always so: when the wall shifts, they move along with it, as you will see in the part on the order of moves.
step.t_safe: The black king, on d5, is in the centre, and your king is still far from it, on g4. A bishop check looks like the natural answer. How do you hold the black king without losing a piece?
step.t_safe.hint1: Before giving check, see who defends the square the piece goes to.
step.t_safe.hint2: There is a king move that faces the black king with one square between them.
step.safe: The checks 1.Be6+ and 1.Bc6+ seem to push the king, but e6 and c6 are next to the black king and no white piece defends those squares. Without the bishop, there is no mate. The white king does the job with no risk: on f5, facing the black king, it takes e4, e5 and e6 at once, and the black king cannot come next to it.
step.d_hang: Watch the reply after 1.Be6+??, the undefended check.
step.d_hang.m1: 1...Kxe6. The black king captures the bishop. King and knight alone cannot mate: it is a draw.
step.safe1: Now the right way: first hold the black king, then bring the bishop.
step.safe1.hint: King in front of the black king, with one square between them. The bishop comes after, to a square your king defends.
step.safe1.done: 1.Kf5! took the opposition. After 1...Kc5, 2.Be6 is now safe: e6 is protected by the king on f5. First the king holds, then the piece comes.
step.safe2: Another position: the black king, on f3, attacks your knight on f2. Where does the knight go?
step.safe2.hint: There is a square next to the black king where the bishop on g6 defends the knight.
step.safe2.done: 1.Ne4! The bishop on g6 defends the knight, and from e4 it still takes f2, g3 and g5 from the black king. It blocks the bishop's diagonal, but the square behind it, d3, already belongs to your king. A protected square is not enough: if it is far from the black king, or if the knight there blocks squares the bishop needs, prefer a square near the black king where the other piece can defend the knight on the next move, preferably with check.
step.t_order: Your pieces are scattered: the bishop on f7, the knight on c6, the king on c3. The black king, on f3, wants to get back to the centre through e3 or e4. Which piece moves first?
step.t_order.hint1: Count how many squares each move takes from the black king.
step.t_order.hint2: The black king needs e3 and e4. Which piece takes both at once?
step.order: A bishop or knight move takes at most one of those two squares. The king takes both, and e5 as well, and the black king cannot attack it. With the pieces scattered, the order decides how many moves you spend: first the move that takes the most squares, without leaving a piece loose.
step.d_wrongOrder: Watch what happens if the bishop moves first.
step.d_wrongOrder.m1: 1.Be6? The bishop closes f5 and g4, but e3 and e4 are still free.
step.d_wrongOrder.m2: 1...Ke4! The black king is back in the centre, right among the white pieces. Four moves lost.
step.order1: Another position, with the pieces scattered: the king on g6, the bishop on c8 and the knight far away, on a4. The black king, on f4, wants the centre. Start with the piece that takes the most squares without leaving any piece loose, and keep squeezing.
step.order1.hint: The king first, taking e5 and g5. The bishop only goes near the black king when your king can defend it.
step.order1.done: 1.Kf6! took e5 and g5; after 1.Be6?, the black king would answer 1...Ke5 and attack the bishop. After 1...Ke4, 2.Be6! closed d5 and f5, protected by the king: the black king cannot get back to the fifth rank. After 2...Kd4, 3.Kf5! took e4 and e5. The knight, far away, comes later.
step.order2: Here the black king is already near the edge, on e7. The count changes: which move takes the most squares now?
step.order2.hint: Which light squares next to the black king are free? One of your pieces takes two of them at once.
step.order2.done: 1.Bc4! took e6 and f7 at once; after 1.Kc7?, the black king would get out with 1...Ke6. After 1...Kd6, 2.Kd8! takes c7 and e7, and the black king is left with c6 only. This time the bishop came first: near the edge, it closes a whole diagonal.
step.t_untangle: The knight, on c2, stands in front of the bishop, between it and the black king. The two pieces get in each other's way, and the black king is right between them. How do you free both without losing time?
step.t_untangle.hint1: If the knight moves away, what does the bishop attack?
step.t_untangle.hint2: Every knight move gives check. Pick a square where the black king cannot capture it and from which it watches the most squares around the black king.
step.untangle: Any knight move opens the bishop's diagonal and gives a discovered check: the black king has to get out of check, and you gain a tempo. The point is where the knight stops. On d4 or e3 it is next to the black king, undefended. Next to the black king only works if another piece defends the square. Among the safe squares, the best is the one that watches the most squares around the black king.
step.d_tangleTrap: Watch the reply after 1.Ne3+??, the check that stops next to the king.
step.d_tangleTrap.m1: 1...Kxe3. The check was discovered, but the knight stopped next to the black king, which captured it. The bishop alone cannot mate: a draw.
step.untangle1.hint: Leave with check to a safe square that watches two squares around the black king; on the next move, bring the knight back close to your king.
step.untangle1.done: 1.Na3+! opened the diagonal with check, on a square the black king cannot reach and from which the knight watches c2 and c4. After 1...Kd4, 2.Nc4! came back, protected by the king on b5, and takes e3, e5 and d2. The bishop, free now, watches the whole diagonal.
step.t_polgar: Monte Carlo, 1994, at the Amber tournament, where grandmasters played blindfold games, without seeing the board. Ljubomir Ljubojević, with White, answered the check 87...Nf4+ with 88.Ke3. You play Black, like Judit Polgár: the pieces are yours now, with the colours swapped. How do you close the white king's way to the centre?
step.t_polgar.hint1: It is the wall from part two, with the colours swapped: the bishop closes the light squares, the knight the dark ones, and the king plugs the rest.
step.t_polgar.hint2: The bishop has to watch d3 and f3 at the same time, on a square your king defends.
step.polgar: How they got here: on move 83, Ljubojević captured Black's last pawn with his rook, and the knight took the rook back with check. Bishop and knight against the lone king were left, and the white king ran to the centre. The defence did what every defender should do: stay in the centre as long as possible and then flee to the wrong corner, a1 or h8, where the light-squared bishop cannot mate. Here, with 88.Ke3?, the white king walked into the net; with 88.Kc3, it would have lasted seven moves longer.
step.d_polgar: The moves that led to this position, from move 84.
step.d_polgar.m1: 84.Kd6. The white king runs to the centre, the defender's first plan.
step.d_polgar.m2: 84...Kf6. The black king follows. There was a faster way, 84...Nf4, but the plan is the same: bring the pieces closer.
step.d_polgar.m3: 85.Kc5. The white king heads for a1, the wrong corner for the light-squared bishop.
step.d_polgar.m4: 85...Ke5. Opposition: the kings face each other with d5 between them. The white king cannot enter the d-file.
step.d_polgar.m5: 86.Kc4. The white king looks for c3 and d3, the road to a1.
step.d_polgar.m6: 86...Bd5+. The bishop pushes with check, protected by the king on e5.
step.d_polgar.m7: 87.Kd3. The white king stays near the centre and can still go to c3, on the way to a1.
step.d_polgar.m8: 87...Nf4+. The knight comes in with check too: from f4 it watches d3, e2 and g2.
step.d_polgar.m9: 88.Ke3? This is the position you studied. The white king walks right among the black pieces; with 88.Kc3, it would have lasted seven moves longer.
step.polgarNet: Now play like Polgár: close the wall with the bishop and push with the king.
step.polgarNet.hint: The bishop goes to the square from which it watches d3 and f3; then the black king steps up to the white king, always taking the square it left.
step.polgarNet.done: Polgár's three moves, 88...Be4!, 89...Kd4! and 90...Kc3!, were the fastest. The white king reached the edge on c1, near a1, the wrong corner. She still drove it all the way to h1, the right corner, and mated on move 106 with 106...Bf3#.
step.t_edge: The black king has reached h8, in the corner, and your king is very close. Now the danger changes: the most natural move can leave the game drawn. Which move must you not play, and what do you play instead?
step.t_edge.hint1: Count the black king's squares after each of your moves.
step.t_edge.hint2: A king with no square and not in check, on its turn, is stalemate: a draw.
step.stalemate: Look at the position after 1.Kf7??, the move that squeezes everything. The white king takes g8 and g7, and the bishop on e4 already watches h7. The black king has no move and is not in check: it is stalemate, and the game ends in a draw.
step.edge1: Now you play. Squeeze the black king, but leave it a square.
step.edge1.hint: Take one square from the black king and leave another free.
step.edge1.done: With 1.Bd5!, for example, the bishop takes g8 and leaves h7: the black king has a move and stays trapped in the corner. What you must not do is take every square without giving check.
step.recap: Three rules to take with you. One: the bishop takes the squares of its colour, the knight those of the other, and the king plugs the rest, with all three pieces always protected. Two: with the pieces scattered, the first move is the one that takes the most squares, very often the king's. Three: the king pushes and the wall moves with it; near the edge, count the black king's squares before squeezing.
step.finish: Your turn, in the practical challenge. The wall is built. Push the black king to the edge and, from there, use what you learnt in the W manoeuvre lesson to finish. If you lose the thread, start again: that is how this ending is learnt.
ex.e04: The black king on c4 wants the centre. Cut it off to the b-file with one move.
ex.e04.hint: The bishop on b2 is on the long diagonal, but behind the king. Bring it to a square from which it takes c5 and c3.
ex.e04.solution: 1.Bd4. The bishop on d4 watches c3 and c5, the knight on d1 watches c3 and e3, the king on e4 watches d3, d4 and d5. The black king is left with b3, b4 and b5: one step from the edge. It is the only move that closes the net at once.
ex.e05: The black king on g3 tries to come back through f2, f3 or f4. Hold it.
ex.e05.hint: The piece that plugs three squares at once is the king. And careful: 1.Bg4 or 1.Bh3 give the bishop away.
ex.e05.solution: 1.Ke3. Opposition: f2, f3 and f4 belong to the white king, g4 and h3 to the bishop, and the black king only has g2, h2 and h4. 1.Bg4 or 1.Bh3 would be captured by the king.
ex.e06: The dark-squared bishop cannot reach d3 or d5. Who covers those two squares?
ex.e06.hint: A knight jump that watches d3 and d5 at the same time.
ex.e06.solution: 1.Nf4. From f4 the knight watches d3 and d5, the light squares the bishop on e3 does not cover; the bishop takes d4 and the white king takes b5 and c5. The black king is pushed to b3, b4 or c3, towards the a-file. 1.Bd4 would lose the bishop.
ex.e07: The black king on b4 is one step from the edge. One king move keeps it there.
ex.e07.hint: Which squares would the black king use to get back to the centre? Take both with the king.
ex.e07.solution: 1.Kd3. The white king takes c3 and c4; the knight on d7 and the bishop on a7 already watch c5 and b6. The black king is stuck on the a- and b-files. Any other move lets the black king out or costs many moves.
ex.e08: The black king on b4 is already close to the a-file. Three precise moves, one with each piece, and it stays trapped there. The order decides.
ex.e08.hint: Start by taking the light squares of the b-file; then the white king steps up, and finally the knight comes to cover the dark squares that are left.
ex.e08.solution: 1.Bc4 takes b3 and b5, and the black king goes to a3. 2.Kc3 takes b2, b3 and b4: a4 is left. 3.Nc2 closes the rest: from c2 the knight watches a3 and b4, the bishop watches b5 and a6, and the black king only has a5. Each move was the only fastest one; changing the order gives the black king a few spare moves.
ex.e09: Bishop and knight are tangled in the a1 corner and the black king on c3 is right among them. Untangle the pieces without losing time: four moves, and each one has to be exact.
ex.e09.hint: The knight blocks the bishop's diagonal. Move the knight out with tempo; then the bishop closes the diagonal and the white king steps up along the d-file and the 6th rank.
ex.e09.solution: 1.Nd3+ is a discovered check from the bishop. After 1...Kc4 (1...Kd2 holds out just as long, and then 2.Bd4 also works), 2.Bd4 takes c3 and c5, and the black king retreats to b5. 3.Kd5 takes c4, c5 and c6, and it goes to a6. 4.Kc6 closes b5, b6 and b7: with the bishop on d4 watching a7, the black king only has a5. Each of these four moves is the only one that gives the black king no time: after any other, it gets back towards the centre and the mate is at least four moves further away.
ex.e10: The black king on c5 is in the centre and your pieces are scattered. Four precise moves to take the centre away from it.
ex.e10.hint: First the king, which takes three squares at once. The knight is far away: bring it to a square that watches e5 and e7. Only then does the bishop close the a2-g8 diagonal.
ex.e10.solution: 1.Kc3 takes b4, c4 and d4, and the black king goes to d6. 2.Ng6 watches e5 and e7, and it comes back to c5. 3.Bc4 closes the diagonal: d5 and b5 belong to the bishop, and the black king retreats to b6. 4.Kb4 takes a5, b5 and c5. The black king is left in the upper corner, behind the bishop's diagonal and the knight's squares, and never gets back to the centre.
ex.e11: The black king on d5 attacks your knight, and your king is far away on a1. Save the knight, but on a square from which it helps to build the net.
ex.e11.hint: On its own, the knight will be attacked again. Look for a square where the bishop can defend it on the next move, and with check.
ex.e11.solution: 1.Nf7. The toughest defence is 1...Ke6, attacking the knight again, but 2.Bc4+ defends it with check. Now the bishop closes the a2-g8 diagonal and the knight on f7 watches d6 and e5: the black king has to step out of check, the knight is already protected, and the white king can come over calmly. Retreats to squares the bishop already guards, such as 1.Nc4 or 1.Nb5, also save the piece but cost moves; 1.Ne4?? loses it, because e4 is next to the black king and nothing defends it.
key.centre: The black king in the centre and the three white pieces crowded in the corner: first they come out and draw closer, then they close the net.
key.far: White's pieces scattered far apart: first the king gains space, then bishop and knight come together to form the barrier.
key.polgar: Monte Carlo, 1994, in a blindfold game: Judit Polgár, with bishop and knight, closes the way to the centre for Ljubomir Ljubojević's king and pushes it to the edge. She mated eighteen moves later.
key.start: The black king in the middle of the white pieces: the first job is to get it out of the centre and towards the edge.
key.wall: Bishop, knight and king together form a wall: the black king can no longer get back to the centre.
history: Bishop and knight against the lone king is the most famous of the hard mates. You would think two extra pieces make it easy, but no: the mate only works in one of the two corners of the bishop's colour, and the king has to be driven there within the fifty-move limit. The ending turns up roughly once in six thousand games, so many players never study it, until it happens to them. Grandmasters have been left with a draw with it on the board: in 2013, in Geneva, Anna Ushenina, then women's world champion, couldn't mate Olga Girya. On the other side, in 1994, in a blindfold game in Monte Carlo, Judit Polgár drove Ljubomir Ljubojević's king from the centre to the edge and gave this mate; and in 1997 the American Tal Shaked beat Alexander Morozevich with it and became world junior champion.
practice: Now the real ending, against the clock or without it. Here the black king is already on the edge, on h3, close to the right corner; the rest is up to you. If you want to start from the centre, open the custom training and build the wall from scratch.
